item.title: Jio Platforms shares trade at 22% premium in grey market ahead of IPO debut
item.description: Jio Platforms' $3.1 billion IPO attracted over $78 billion in bids, while its grey market premium held near 22% ahead of its October 28 debut ...
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: For investors lucky enough to land shares in Jio Platforms Ltd.’s $3.1 billion India-record initial public offering, trading on the unofficial market is fueling hopes of a big debut pop. Billionaire Mukesh Ambani’s digital and telecommunications giant has attracted stellar demand across investor categories ahead of its Oct. 28 market debut. Investors who got their allocations on Tuesday are now closely watching Jio’s gray-market pricing for clues about how the first day might unfold. The premium over the IPO price has hovered at about 22% for roughly 10 days, unusually resilient for an offering of this size, according to the ipowatch.in and investorgain.com platforms.  Gray market premiums are unregulated and provide no guarantee of where a stock will actually trade once it hits the exchange. Still, they are widely tracked in India as a barometer of demand and listing-day sentiment. If the pattern holds into the listing, it would make Jio India’s second-most valuable company after parent Reliance Industries Ltd., pushing rival Bharti Airtel Ltd. into third place. That prospect is adding to the excitement around an IPO that’s already rewritten records in India’s capital markets. Jio attracted more than $78 billion in bids and nearly 14 million applications in one of the country’s most anticipated listings.  So far, Jio has been able to defy the usual trend of gray market premiums cooling after an IPO closes, as the initial rush of bidding fades and investors shift their focus to allotments and the eventual listing. After National Stock Exchange of India Ltd.’s $2.4 billion IPO, the premium gradually eroded from about 15% to 3% in two weeks and the shares ultimately made a relatively muted debut.The optimism is backed by blockbuster subscription numbers. Jio’s IPO was subscribed more than 22 times, with qualified institutional buyers bidding for 71 times the shares reserved for them. Wealthy investors subscribed 14 times their allocation, while the retail portion was covered 2.7 times. The offering was fully subscribed within just 100 minutes of opening last week, even as a bruising selloff swept through Indian equities.

item.title: The Fed is expected to hold rates steady. Warsh will have to explain why
item.description: The Federal Reserve is expected to hold rates steady as inflation pressures persist, with Kevin Warsh facing questions over the timing of further rate hikes ...
item.dc:creator: NYT
item.content:encoded: By Colby  smith Kevin M Warsh wants inflation to move more swiftly back to the Federal Reserve’s (Fed’s) 2 per cent target. But on Wednesday, the central bank chairman and his colleagues are widely expected to hold interest rates steady. The discrepancy is poised to be a focal point at the latest meeting, which is taking place just days before midterm elections that will decide who controls Congress in the latter half of President Trump’s second term. Since officials voted unanimously in September to raise rates by a quarter of a percentage point to 3.75 per cent to 4 per cent, the incoming inflation data has been anything but reassuring. Energy prices are up across the board as the war with Iran has dragged on. The range of goods and services growing costlier appears to be broadening. And a splurge in spending tied to the proliferation of artificial intelligence (AI) shows little sign of abating. The Fed’s other priority, the labour market, has also remained stable, despite monthly growth slowing in September, a sign that Fed’s policy settings are not excessively onerous for the economy. Numerous Fed policymakers have already indicated their support for a rate increase at their final gathering of the year in December in pursuit of a “timelier” return to the 2 per cent target after six years of overshooting it. So the question for Warsh at Wednesday’s news conference is: why wait? Warsh had the last word ahead of the upcoming rate decision. Speaking in Bangkok at the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank this month, the chairman did little to change the narrative laid out by a number of his fellow policymakers in the preceding weeks. The overarching message was that the central bank had more work to do to tame inflation, but there was no urgency to raise rates at consecutive meetings. But for a broad swathe of economists and investors, the primary reason a rate increase was not pencilled in for October, despite hotter-than-expected inflation data, was precisely the steer provided by Warsh’s colleagues. Recent jitters in financial markets amid concerns about the sustainability of the AI boom have also helped. That has made financial conditions, which measure the availability of credit in the economy, only slightly less accommodative than before. But looking solely at the inflation data, Riccardo Trezzi, a former Fed economist who runs the research firm Underlying Inflation, said a rate increase was clearly justified on Wednesday. “There is zero evidence of cooling down,” he said of current price pressures. Trezzi estimates that the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, which strips out volatile food and energy items, will reach 3.4 per cent in December. At the same time last year, it stood at 3 per cent. Overall inflation, as measured by the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index, is projected to reach 3.8 per cent, according to Trezzi’s calculations, nearly double the 2 per cent target. PCE data for September will be released on Thursday, the day after the Fed’s decision. “There’s a disconnect in terms of how the Fed sounds at the moment,” he said. “They still have to make up their minds whether they’re really serious about disinflating the US economy.” The issue for the Fed is that the primary sources of resurgent inflation are beyond its control. Beyond the Iran war and Trump’s tariffs, both of which have added to price pressures, many of the biggest AI companies fuelling growth also appear impervious to higher rates. Perhaps the biggest driver of demand right now is the sharp rise in wealth across the country generated by stock market gains, said Marc Sumerlin of Evenflow Macro, an economic consulting firm. In the last four quarters, households’ net worth rose roughly $20 trillion, according to Fed data as of September. While most of these gains have accrued to high-income households, this group drives the bulk of consumer spending. Estimates vary on how much the Fed will need to squeeze the economy in the coming months to begin turning the tide on inflation. Some believe price pressures will begin to ease as the impact of Trump’s tariffs and the energy shock fades, removing the need for an aggressive response from the Fed. But others believe a more forceful approach might be required. The first of two wild cards is how financial conditions evolve in the coming months. US government bond yields are sharply higher today than they were just a few months ago for a variety of reasons. Some of that reflects changing expectations about how much the Fed will need to raise rates as growth has picked up. There is also intensifying competition between governments and companies for capital as large AI companies borrow aggressively to fund their expansions. Investors also appear to be demanding extra compensation to hold longer-dated debt rather than shorter-term securities amid persistent concerns about Washington’s fiscal profligacy and fluctuating worries about the Fed’s ability to operate independently, said Ellen Zentner, chief economic strategist at Morgan Stanley Wealth Management.  Rising yields will marginally help the Fed pursue its inflation goal, but that will not entirely replace the work the central bank has to do to raise rates to at least a neutral level, which neither speeds up nor slows down the economy, Zentner said. The second wild card is how the public perceives the Fed’s grip on inflation. Concerns about price pressures in the year ahead have mounted, but longer-term indicators look more benign.  For now, that has afforded the Fed some flexibility over when it must deliver additional increases, said Raphael Bostic, who served as president of the Atlanta Fed for nine years until February. But “there are limits”, he warned.

item.content:encoded:
Home / Markets / News / Sebi extends compliance deadline for debenture trustees till April 2027

Sebi extends compliance deadline for debenture trustees till April 2027 Markets regulator Sebi on Tuesday extended the deadline by six months, till April 27, 2027, for debenture trustees to comply with requirements governing activities that fall outside its regulatory purview.

Sebi has extended the compliance deadline for debenture trustees by six months to April 27, 2027. (Photo: Reuters)

PTI New Delhi 2 min read Last Updated : Oct 27 2026 | 11:59 PM IST

Listen to This Article

Markets regulator Sebi on Tuesday extended the deadline by six months, till April 27, 2027, for debenture trustees to comply with requirements governing activities that fall outside its regulatory purview. Under Regulation 9C of the Sebi (Debenture Trustees) Regulations, 1993, a debenture trustee holding a valid certificate of registration is required to transfer activities not regulated by the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) to separate business units within a prescribed timeline. The provision was introduced through amendments notified on October 27, 2025, to provide clarity on the scope of activities permitted for debenture trustees. Sebi had initially given six months for compliance. Subsequently, in April 2026, the regulator granted an additional six months, extending the deadline to October 27, 2026, following industry representations highlighting operational challenges in establishing the necessary systems and processes.

In its latest circular on Tuesday, Sebi has "decided to grant an additional period of six months (i.e. up to April 27, 2027) to DTs for ensuring compliance with the said requirements". Also Read

The additional extension was granted in view of a comprehensive review of the regulatory framework for debenture trustees being undertaken by an Expert Working Group (EWG) constituted in June 2026. The working group is examining the existing regulatory framework applicable to debenture trusteeship activities, including aspects related to the Separate Business Unit (SBU) framework, as well as other incidental matters. The regulator also considered representations from debenture trustee associations highlighting challenges in implementing the SBU-related guidelines.

"Considering that the EWG is undertaking a comprehensive review of the regulatory framework for DTs, including aspects related to the SBU framework, and further representations received from DT Associations highlighting the challenges in the implementation of SBU-related guidelines, the EWG decided to grant an additional period of six months (i.e. up to April 27, 2027) to DTs for ensuring compliance with the said requirements," Sebi said.

item.content:encoded:
Home / Economy / News / No pressure from US to reduce Russian oil imports, says Hardeep Puri

No pressure from US to reduce Russian oil imports, says Hardeep Puri India's imports of West Asian crude oil surged in September, returning to pre-war levels, while its refiners cut back purchases of Russian oil amid stiff competition from China

Hardeep Puri said West Asia oil supplies have been rising as the region is able to ship out more cargoes

Reuters GOA 2 min read Last Updated : Oct 27 2026 | 12:49 PM IST

Listen to This Article

India has faced no pressure from the US to reduce its Russian crude imports, oil minister Hardeep Singh Puri said on Tuesday at an industry event.   "I never felt anything," Puri said when asked if there has been pressure to cut Russian oil imports.   Puri said West Asia oil supplies have been rising as the region is able to ship out more cargoes.   He said India was getting 0.2% of its oil imports from Russia before the Ukraine war, while imports have surged since the war started due to discounts on Russian oil.   India's imports of West Asian crude oil surged in September, returning to pre-war levels, while its refiners cut back purchases of Russian oil amid stiff competition from China, ship-tracking data showed.

Also Read

The minister said that the purchase of Russian oil is linked to discounts and pricing when compared with other grades. Russian oil imports have been reduced as the refiners are buying more Gulf oil sold at a discount, he added.   "Whatever people say or do, ultimately it is anchored in their self-interest," he said.   The minister also said India is expanding its refining capacity to help meet local demand and export commitments.

(Only the headline and picture of this report may have been reworked by the Business Standard staff; the rest of the content is auto-generated from a syndicated feed.)
